newsitem.title: USA: Miami draws foreign firms with eye to Latam business.
newsitem.headline: Miami draws foreign firms with eye to Latam business.

text.p: Miami's role as the business hub of Latin America has drawn not only offices of U.S. and Latin American corporations, but those of companies from Europe, Canada and other parts of the world.

"We see Miami as one of the parts of a triangle. The other two are Europe and Latin America," said George Van Klan, co-chairman of the Greater Miami Chamber of Commerce Europe/Middle East Committee and a recently retired executive from Johnson & Johnson.

The city's stability, large Spanish-speaking population and location attract foreign firms just as they do the Latin American offices of U.S. companies, from Texaco Inc. to AT&T Corp. to MTV, said executives attending a recent Greater Miami Chamber of Commerce conference on marketing in Latin America.

Germany will be sponsoring a trade show in Miami on Latin American trade opportunities soon. More than 100 foreign investors were in Miami Beach this week for the International Real Estate Congress. EFE, the Spanish news agency, just announced plans for a large Miami-based office.

David Ericson, commercial officer for the Canadian Consulate, said dozens of Canadian companies, including the Royal Bank of Canada, Air Canada, and many smaller firms have offices in southern Florida.
"There are more than you might think," he said.
Experts said the Florida city was the logical choice for companies doing business with any Latin American nation, except Mexico, which is much closer to Texas and California.

"Miami positioned itself as the bridge, so any foreign company that wants to market simultaneously to the north and south, they come to Miami," said Hedy Nuraef, chief executive and special projects director at HNZ Marketsearch, a Latin American research firm.

Economist and business strategists said they view Latin America as a largely untapped multibillion-dollar market, although one that can offer high risks and, as more and more foreign companies move in, stiff competition.
Nuraef said her research has shown that Latin American companies, many of which are recently privatised, are far behind their U.S. counterparts' sales and marketing techniques.
"They don't know how to compete," she said. "Marketing is an American invention."

Antonio Villamil, president of the Washington Economics Group, and a former U.S. undersecretary of commerce and chief economist, said Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and Venezuela were top markets for foreign companies. He added that companies could also profit by looking carefully at a tier of "emerging markets," which he said included Peru, El Salvador, Bolivia, Ecaudor, Panama, Costa Rica, Guatemala and Nicaragua.

"Nicaragua could be a sleeper under President Arnoldo Aleman," he said, giving one example. "In the next three to five years, you are going to see that market, under Aleman, much better than it is today," he said, praising the conservative president's economic policies.

He said other countries close to Miami could be attractive "niche" markets for careful investors, among them the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Honduras, and Trinidad and Tobago. The latter, he said "has become really the capital for the eastern Caribbean."
